codex_planning_prompt.role: You are a senior software architect and technical lead. You are being handed a greenfield project to design (not yet build) a replacement Point-of-Sale (POS) and back-office system for a brick-and-mortar farm-supply retailer. Treat this as a high-stakes business-critical system: the store transacts cash and cards every day, and the system it currently depends on is being shut off. Reliability, payment security, and a clean cutover are paramount.
codex_planning_prompt.critical_directive: DO NOT WRITE ANY APPLICATION CODE IN THIS RESPONSE. Your sole deliverable is a detailed, structured implementation plan as described in . You may write illustrative data-model sketches, API endpoint lists, and pseudo-flow, but no real implementation. Before any build phase begins, the plan must be reviewed and approved by a human (the RuneStoneLabs team). End your response with the open questions you need answered before execution. If a requirement is ambiguous, state your assumption explicitly rather than guessing silently.
codex_planning_prompt.objective: Produce a complete, phased plan to replace the Hatchers retail POS and back-office system. The new system must: (1) run in-store checkout reliably, (2) fix the two biggest pain points of the old system — inventory management and customer/loyalty — and (3) integrate with the merchant's existing payment processor, TSYS, for card-present payments.

business_context.company: Hatchers — a retailer of landscape and livestock supplies, comparable to a Southern States farm co-op / agricultural supply store.
business_context.model: Card-present, brick-and-mortar retail. Customers walk in, build a cart of physical goods (bagged feed, seed, fertilizer, mulch, hardware, animal-health products, etc.), and check out at a register. In-store transactions are the dominant channel. Do NOT assume e-commerce is out of scope: Bindo offered an online storefront, so first determine via the feature-parity audit whether this store actually sells online today. If it does, replacing or deliberately sunsetting that storefront is in scope and must be planned, not dropped silently.
business_context.built_by: RuneStoneLabs LLC — a small software shop. Assume a two-developer team with limited bandwidth. The plan should be realistic for a small team and favor proven, low-maintenance technology over novelty.

current_state.legacy_pos: Bindo POS. Bindo has gone out of business / shut down its service, which is the forcing function for this migration. The merchant must be off Bindo before service ends.
current_state.payment_processor: TSYS (the merchant's existing processor). The new system must continue using TSYS so the merchant keeps their existing merchant account, rates, and funding.

pain_points.pain: Inventory management — the old system's inventory handling was inadequate. This is a primary reason for switching and must be a first-class feature, not an afterthought.
Customer / loyalty — customer records and loyalty/rewards were weak. The new system needs real customer accounts, purchase history, and a loyalty mechanism.
Vendor risk — Bindo shutting down stranded the business. The plan should favor self-hostable / portable architecture so the merchant is never again held hostage by a single vendor's survival.

feature_parity_audit.directive: Before designing anything, establish FULL FEATURE PARITY with what Bindo actually does for THIS store today. The pain points above are the reasons for switching, not the full scope. The greatest migration risk is silently dropping a capability the store relies on daily. Do not assume the requirements listed elsewhere in this prompt are exhaustive — they are not. Your job is to discover everything the store currently gets from Bindo and make a deliberate, documented decision about each one: replicate it, replace it (e.g., via a third-party integration), drop it (with the merchant's explicit sign-off), or defer it to a later phase.
feature_parity_audit.source_of_truth: The authoritative source for "what services Bindo provides to this customer" is what THIS store actually uses — captured before Bindo's service ends. Drive a current-state audit: interview the owner and front-line staff, walk the live Bindo system screen by screen while it is still accessible, review their existing receipts/reports/back-office, and inventory every Bindo feature, report, and integration in active use. Treat any still-accessible Bindo account as a time-limited asset — capture screenshots, exports, and configuration now.

bindo_capability_checklist.note: Bindo's known capability set. Use as a probe list during the audit — for EACH item, determine whether this store uses it and whether the new system must cover it. Presence in this list does not mean the store uses it; absence does not mean it can be skipped.
bindo_capability_checklist.item: In-store checkout / smart register, cash management, end-of-day
Inventory management, purchase orders, receiving, reorder/par levels, real-time stock
Product matrix / variants (attributes such as size, color, material)
Barcode/UPC catalog with auto-populated product photo/title/description
Customer CRM, profiles, and full purchase history
Loyalty / rewards program
Gift cards (branded, balance tracking, redemption) — distinct from loyalty and house accounts
Store credit
Promotions / discount engine, smart promotion recommendations, upsell/related items
Email / SMS marketing and targeted campaigns
Online storefront / e-commerce (Bindo could add a webstore to an existing site)
Omnichannel / online-to-offline order management; the Bindo Marketplace consumer app
Mobile POS (mPOS) — selling from a tablet/handheld on the sales floor
Store-and-forward OFFLINE mode (process card sales during an internet outage)
QuickBooks and/or Xero accounting integration / financial sync
Employee management and timeclock / hours tracking
Real-time analytics dashboard, KPI/visual reporting, sales and inventory reports
Multi-store management
Hardware: receipt printer, barcode scanner, cash drawer, card terminal, customer display
API access / third-party integrations the store depends on

feature_parity_audit.special_attention: Two items are explicitly flagged because losing them silently would be a real regression: (1) ONLINE STOREFRONT — if the store sells online via Bindo, do not assume e-commerce is out of scope; surface it and plan for replacement or a deliberate, signed-off sunset. (2) STORE-AND-FORWARD OFFLINE MODE — Bindo could keep selling during an internet outage; the replacement must meet or beat this. Treat it as existing parity, not a new nice-to-have.
feature_parity_audit.output: Produce a Feature Parity Matrix (required in the plan output) listing every Bindo capability the store uses, with: in-use? (yes/no/unknown), disposition (replicate / replace-via-integration / drop / defer), target phase, owner of the decision, and rationale. Anything marked "drop" or "defer" must be explicitly confirmed by the merchant, not decided unilaterally.

codex_planning_prompt.technical_stack_baseline: The RuneStoneLabs default stack is the starting point. Use it unless POS-specific realities (offline operation, hardware peripherals, payment terminals) make a different choice clearly better — in which case, call that out and justify it. Node.js / Express PostgreSQL with Prisma ORM React with Vite Railway, GitHub push-to-deploy CI/CD This is a cloud-deployed stack, but a POS for a physical store has constraints a normal web SaaS does not (see ). Explicitly address how an in-store register keeps selling when the internet connection drops. Do not assume always-online.

functional_requirements.checkout: Register/lane checkout flow: item lookup by SKU/barcode scan and by search; cart with quantity, line discounts, and order-level discounts; multiple tender types (cash, card via TSYS terminal, store/house account charge, check, split tender); change calculation; void, return, and refund flows; receipt printing (and optional email/SMS receipt); cash drawer open/close and end-of-day reconciliation (Z-report).
functional_requirements.inventory: First-class inventory: products with SKU, barcode/UPC, category/department, supplier, cost, retail price; stock-on-hand tracking with automatic decrement on sale and increment on receiving; reorder points and low-stock alerts; purchase orders to suppliers and goods-receiving; stock adjustments (shrinkage, damage, count corrections); physical inventory / cycle counting. Account for farm-supply realities: items sold by weight and by unit, bulk/pallet quantities, bundle/kit items, and seasonal stocking.
functional_requirements.reporting: Sales reporting (by day, item, category, register, employee); inventory valuation and movement reports; tax reports; customer/loyalty reports; export to CSV/spreadsheet. Reporting was a generic weakness of small-shop POS — make exports easy.
functional_requirements.users_and_roles: Employee accounts with role-based permissions (cashier vs. manager vs. owner), clock-in identity on transactions, and an audit trail for voids, refunds, discounts, and price overrides.

domain_specific_requirements.note: These are easy to overlook and expensive to retrofit. Plan for them in the data model from day one.
domain_specific_requirements.house_accounts: Charge / house accounts: many farm-supply customers buy on store credit with net-30 (or similar) terms. Need per-customer credit limits, running balances, statements, aging (30/60/90), and the ability to apply payments against an account. This is effectively a lightweight accounts-receivable subsystem and must be designed in, not bolted on.
domain_specific_requirements.tax_exemption: Agricultural / resale tax exemption: farmers frequently hold ag tax-exemption certificates. The system must store exemption certificates per customer, apply tax exemption at checkout, and report on exempt vs. taxable sales for compliance. Plan how exemptions interact with the tax engine.
domain_specific_requirements.pricing_tiers: Multiple price levels: retail vs. wholesale/commercial/contractor pricing, plus quantity and bulk-break pricing. A given customer may be assigned a price tier.
domain_specific_requirements.special_orders: Special orders / non-stock items the store orders in for a customer, including deposits and customer notification on arrival.
domain_specific_requirements.units_of_measure: Flexible units of measure: each, bag, pallet, ton, pound, foot, etc., with conversions where a product is bought in one unit and sold in another.

payment_integration_tsys.directive: Integrate with TSYS for card-present payments using a SEMI-INTEGRATED payment terminal architecture. The POS application MUST NOT capture, transmit, or store raw cardholder data. Card data flows from the customer-facing certified terminal directly to TSYS for authorization; the POS sends the amount to the terminal and receives back an approval/decline and non-sensitive receipt data. This keeps the POS out of PCI-DSS scope and avoids EMV brand certification.
payment_integration_tsys.research_required: Identify and recommend the specific TSYS integration path and terminal hardware. Investigate TSYS / Global Payments semi-integrated offerings (e.g., TSYS Multipass for connecting a front-end to TSYS processing, TSYS Genius, and TSYS auth/host-capture platforms such as Sierra / Transit) and certified semi-integrated terminals (PAX, Ingenico, Dejavoo, Equinox). Confirm which path supports card-present EMV chip, contactless/NFC, and debit, and which is realistically obtainable for a small merchant on an existing TSYS account. Note that TSYS is now part of Global Payments; verify current product names and integration toolkits rather than assuming legacy branding.
payment_integration_tsys.must_support: EMV chip, contactless/tap, swipe fallback, debit with PIN, partial approvals, refunds/voids tied back to the original transaction, and end-of-day batch settlement.
payment_integration_tsys.deliverable: The plan must include: the recommended TSYS integration approach with justification, the terminal hardware shortlist, the request/response flow between POS and terminal, the onboarding/certification steps required with TSYS, and an explicit statement of the resulting PCI-DSS scope and SAQ type for the merchant.

data_migration_bindo.risk: Bindo has shut down. Getting data OUT of Bindo may be difficult or time-limited. Treat data extraction as a named risk with a fallback plan, not an assumption.
data_migration_bindo.required: Plan how to extract and migrate: product catalog (SKUs, barcodes, prices, costs, categories), current inventory quantities, customer records, house-account balances, and historical sales (at minimum recent history for reporting continuity). Address: available Bindo export formats or reports, whether any data must be recovered from backups/receipts/spreadsheets, data cleaning and de-duplication, a validation/reconciliation step, and a fallback if a clean export is not obtainable (e.g., manual catalog rebuild, barcode re-scanning, opening counts).

constraints.offline_resilience: The store cannot stop selling if the internet goes down. Define the offline strategy: can the register operate in a degraded local mode and sync when connectivity returns? What is the source of truth for inventory and prices locally vs. in the cloud? How are card payments handled offline (typically the terminal/processor governs this — clarify)? This is a core architectural decision and may push back on the pure cloud-web baseline; address it head-on.
constraints.pci_dss: Minimize PCI scope via the semi-integrated terminal design above. State the target SAQ and the controls required. The POS database must never contain PAN or sensitive authentication data.
constraints.peripherals: Plan for in-store hardware: barcode scanner, receipt printer, cash drawer, customer-facing card terminal, and optionally a label/price-tag printer and a scale for by-weight items. Specify how a web/React front-end will talk to these peripherals (e.g., browser-supported hardware, a local bridge/agent, or a thin native shell) and recommend an approach.
constraints.multi_lane: Support more than one register/lane in the store running concurrently against shared inventory, and design so a second store location could be added later without a rewrite.
constraints.portability: Favor self-hostable, vendor-portable architecture so the merchant is never stranded again by a vendor shutdown (the Bindo lesson). Avoid hard lock-in to any single proprietary platform beyond the unavoidable payment processor relationship.

assumptions.note: Stated so they can be corrected; do not treat as confirmed fact.
assumptions.assumption: Single store location for v1, designed to scale to multiple locations later.
In-store card-present is the primary payment channel; no online checkout in v1.
The merchant retains and keeps using their existing TSYS merchant account.
RuneStoneLabs hosts the system (likely on Railway) and maintains it for the merchant under a managed/retainer model.

codex_planning_prompt.required_plan_output:
Produce the plan in the following structure. Be specific and concrete; avoid generic filler.
One page: what is being built, the chosen architecture at a high level, the biggest risks, and the recommended phasing.
The questions that must be answered before building, grouped by topic (business rules, TSYS account specifics, hardware, data migration, hosting).
Components and how they connect; offline/online strategy; how registers, the back office, the database, and the payment terminal relate. Include a clear diagram-in-text or component list. Justify any deviation from the baseline stack.
Core entities and key relationships (products, inventory, customers, house accounts, sales/line items, tenders, suppliers, purchase orders, users, tax/exemption, pricing tiers, loyalty). Sketch tables/fields; flag where PCI scope is avoided.
Each functional area broken into concrete capabilities, each tagged MVP / v1 / later.
Recommended integration path and terminal, the POS↔terminal flow, certification/onboarding steps, and resulting PCI scope.
Extraction approach, cleaning, validation, reconciliation, and fallback.
Realistic phases for a small team, each with goals, scope, and an exit/acceptance criterion. Identify the minimum cutover-ready milestone (the point at which the store could run a full business day on the new system).
How to switch the store from Bindo to the new system with minimal downtime, including a rollback/contingency if go-live fails.
Ranked risks (Bindo data availability, TSYS certification timeline, offline behavior, hardware compatibility, team bandwidth) with mitigations.
Everything you need answered before writing code.
codex_planning_prompt.final_instruction: Think holistically before writing. Optimize the plan for a small team delivering a reliable, cutover-ready store system on a deadline driven by Bindo's shutdown. When you finish, do not start building — stop at the plan and wait for human approval.
